papers.title: Anomalous Field-induced Coherence beyond Single-ion Kondo Physics
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31137v1

summary.one_liner: In the Ce-based heavy fermion Ce2Rh3Ga5, a magnetic field produces large negative magnetoresistance and restores T^2 coherent transport, a behavior the authors say cannot be explained by single-ion Kondo physics alone and resembles the anomalous magnetotransport of UBe13.
summary.plain: Some metals made of rare-earth elements carry heavy electrons that usually conduct electricity more easily as they get colder. This paper studies Ce2Rh3Ga5, a material whose electrical resistance stays high at very low temperatures, and reports that a magnetic field lowers that resistance and makes the material behave like a well-ordered metal again. The authors conclude that a simple single-atom model does not account for the drop, which points to an extra source of electron scattering.
summary.why: The result matters because it offers a new, clean material in which electron scattering and coherent transport can be studied in a heavy fermion system without superconductivity, which complicates the older UBe13 case. The text does not establish the microscopic origin of the extra scattering, so its broader significance is still to be tested.
summary.background:
- Heavy fermions: metals whose electrons behave as if they are many times heavier than normal, usually arising from interactions with localized magnetic atoms (here cerium).
- Kondo effect: a localized magnetic atom gets screened by conduction electrons; the single-ion version describes one such atom at a time.
- Coherence: when scattering weakens and electrons act collectively, resistivity typically drops at low temperature.
- Resistivity and magnetoresistance: resistance to electric current, and how much it changes with a magnetic field.
- Specific heat coefficient C/T: a measure of how many low-energy thermal states the electrons have; large values signal heavy quasiparticles.
- T^2 resistivity: resistance that grows with the square of temperature, a signature of coherent metallic behavior.
- UBe13: a uranium heavy fermion compound with long-standing puzzles in its transport, which the paper uses as a comparison.

papers.abstract: The emergence of coherent heavy quasiparticles in Kondo lattices is generally accompanied by a reduction in electrical resistivity at low temperatures. However, certain strongly correlated metals exhibit anomalously large resistivities that persist to very low temperatures, raising fundamental questions about the mechanisms governing charge transport. Here, we report an unusual magnetic field-induced evolution of electronic transport and thermodynamic properties in a Ce-based heavy fermion compound, Ce$_{2}$Rh$_{3}$Ga$_{5}$. At zero field, Ce$_{2}$Rh$_{3}$Ga$_{5}$ undergoes a magnetic transition at $T$$_{0}$ = 0.45 K and exhibits a strongly enhanced low temperature specific heat coefficient, reaching $C$/$T$ = 2.2 J/mol$_{Ce}$-K$^{2}$, but no discernible coherence in its electrical resistivity. Remarkably, applying a magnetic field produces a large negative magnetoresistance and restores coherent metallic behavior, characterized by low-temperature $T$$^2$ resistivity. Although the field dependence of the electronic specific heat coefficient can be described phenomenologically within a single-ion Kondo framework, the same description fails to account for the strong suppression of the residual resistivity and the overall magnetoresistance. These results point to an additional field-sensitive scattering contribution beyond conventional single-ion Kondo physics. The striking resemblance to the long-standing anomalous magnetotransport behavior of UBe$_{13}$, without the complications introduced by superconductivity, establishes Ce$_{2}$Rh$_{3}$Ga$_{5}$ as a platform for investigating the microscopic origin of anomalous scattering and field-induced coherent transport in strongly correlated electron systems.

papers.title: Perfect Spin-to-Charge Signal Conversion via Inverse Spin Hall Effect in a Superconductor
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30781v1

summary.one_liner: A theoretical proposal that, in a superconductor, the quasiparticle charge imbalance created by injected spin accumulation can convert spin into a charge voltage near unity efficiency via the inverse spin Hall effect, despite a small spin Hall angle, with finite broadening and temperature effects included.
summary.plain: Spintronics devices often turn spin (a quantum magnetic property of electrons) into an electrical voltage, but the usual materials convert only a small fraction of it. This paper argues that running the process through a superconductor, a material that carries current without resistance below a critical temperature, could make the voltage almost as large as the injected spin signal. The authors derive the full theory of this effect for a standard test geometry and suggest experiments that vary temperature and spin bias to check it.
summary.why: If confirmed, a near-complete spin-to-charge conversion would be a useful readout tool for spin-based electronics, which is why the claim merits attention. The text is theoretical only and reports no experimental data, so the size of the effect in real materials remains untested.
summary.background:
- Spin: an electron's intrinsic magnetic moment, which can be carried as a "spin accumulation" in a material.
- Spin Hall effect / inverse spin Hall effect: a spin current bends sideways and produces a transverse charge voltage; the spin Hall angle measures how efficient this is, and it is usually small.
- Nonlocal spin-valve: a device where spin is injected at one point and detected by a voltage at a separate point, so the signal is not mixed with ordinary charge current.
- Superconductor gap: below a critical temperature, electrons pair up and there is an energy gap; quasiparticles (single unpaired excitations) are suppressed below this gap, so charge current flows with little resistance.
- Charge imbalance: a surplus of one kind of quasiparticle charge that a spin bias can create in a superconductor.
- Spectral broadening: a smearing of the energy levels caused by finite lifetimes, which the paper includes in its calculation.

papers.abstract: Spin-to-charge conversion is central to spintronics, but conventional spin Hall mechanisms are intrinsically limited by the small spin Hall angle. Here we show that superconductivity can overcome this limitation and enable near-unity spin-to-charge signal conversion. We consider a nonlocal spin-valve geometry in which a spin accumulation is injected into a superconductor and converted into a transverse charge signal through the inverse spin Hall effect. In the superconducting state, the strongly suppressed quasiparticle conductance below the gap allows the resulting charge imbalance to generate a voltage comparable to the injected spin bias, despite a small spin Hall angle. We derive the full nonequilibrium response including finite spectral broadening and finite temperature, and propose temperature and spin-bias-dependent measurements of the detector voltage to test our predictions.

papers.title: Quantum Hall Effect in a 3D Cross-Dimensional Quantum Anomalous Hall System
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28751v1

summary.background:
- Quantum Hall effect: quantized electrical resistance in a material under a magnetic field, carried by one-way edge currents.
- Chern number: an integer that counts topological twist in a material's electronic bands; it predicts how many one-way edge channels exist.
- Bulk-boundary correspondence: the principle that the interior topology determines what happens at a material's surface or edge.
- Weyl semimetal: a 3D material whose electrons behave like massless particles at points in momentum space, the building block here.
- Quantum anomalous Hall effect: a quantized Hall response produced without an external magnetic field, through internal magnetism.
- Multi-terminal transport: measuring currents and voltages at several electrical contacts to map how current flows.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical study of how magnetic fields along three high-symmetry directions change Chern numbers, chiral edge-like modes, and multi-terminal Hall responses in a 3D system built by coupling two Weyl-semimetal Hamiltonians, reporting a breakdown of conventional Chern-number-based bulk-boundary correspondence.
summary.plain: This paper studies a three-dimensional material model that shows the quantum Hall effect, a precisely quantized electrical response usually seen in flat two-dimensional systems. The authors apply magnetic fields along three special directions and track how the topological counts (Chern numbers) and the paths electrons can travel along the surfaces change. They report that the usual rule linking the bulk count to the surface behavior does not fully hold here, and they check this with computer simulations of Hall transport.
summary.why: It challenges a standard rule that topological physicists use to predict edge behavior, which matters for interpreting Hall measurements in 3D materials. The text does not show experimental realization or applications, so its practical reach is unclear.

papers.abstract: We systematically investigate cross-dimensional transport and the resulting quantum Hall effect in 3D quantum anomalous Hall effect systems, which are constructed by coupling two Weyl-semimetal Hamiltonians. Our study unveils that the system hosts highly anisotropic surface states and chiral modes, leading to rich quantum Hall responses. Crucially, we clarify how magnetic fields applied along three high-symmetry directions dictate the evolution of the Chern numbers, chiral modes, and Hall responses. We discover that chiral modes along different directions can originate from distinct mechanisms, giving rise to various magnetic modulation characteristics. Furthermore, we unveil the breakdown of the conventional Chern-number-based bulk-boundary correspondence under magnetic fields, where the Chern numbers alone fail to fully characterize the evolution of the chiral states. This anomalous behavior is attributed to the unique momentum-space distributions of surface bands. These insights are further validated numerically through multi-terminal Hall transport simulations. Our findings expand the understanding of magnetic-field-driven mechanisms in 3D topological systems and provide deeper insights into the interplay between quantized Hall effects and Chern numbers in 3D systems.

papers.title: Floquet-Induced Valley Polarization and Topological Phases in Twisted Bilayer Graphene Heterostructures
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28797v1

summary.background:
- Graphene: a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon; stacking two sheets with a small twist angle creates a "moiré" pattern that changes how electrons behave.
- Valley: a distinct low-energy momentum point in the electron band structure; "valley degree of freedom" means electrons can carry information in which valley they occupy.
- Dirac-like dispersion: electrons behaving like massless particles, with energy rising linearly with momentum; this gives conducting behavior.
- Band gap: an energy range with no allowed electron states; a gapped valley is effectively switched off.
- Floquet driving: treating a periodically oscillating light field as creating an effective, modified material during illumination.
- Inversion symmetry: a symmetry where the structure looks the same when flipped through a central point; breaking it is needed for the valley effects.
- Chern number: an integer describing the topological character of electron bands; changes signal topological phase transitions.
- Domain-wall channel: a boundary between differently ordered regions that conducts electrons along it.
- Spin-valley filtering: selecting electrons by spin and valley type.
summary.one_liner: A theoretical study of twisted bilayer graphene under circularly polarized light, with broken inversion symmetry from an out-of-plane electric field and insulating substrates, reporting Floquet-induced valley polarization, Chern-number phase transitions (C = -2, -1, 0), valley-polarized domain-wall channels, and spin-valley filtering via adjacent 2D ferromagnetic contacts.
summary.plain: This paper is a computer-based theory study of a stack of two sheets of carbon atoms (graphene) twisted relative to each other. Shining circularly polarized light on the stack, and tilting its symmetry with an electric field and surrounding materials, the authors find conditions where one of the two "valleys" (electron energy-momentum sites) stays conducting while the other opens an energy gap and goes quiet. The text reports that this setup can produce topological phase changes and channels that carry only one valley's electrons, and that nearby magnetic layers may allow filtering by spin and valley.
summary.why: It is a proposal for controlling electron valley and spin with light and fields in a tunable material, which may matter for future electronics concepts. The text is theoretical only and gives no experimental confirmation, so the practical relevance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We theoretically investigate twisted bilayer graphene (tTBG) heterostructures subjected to circularly polarized light. Inversion symmetry is broken through the combined application of an out-of-plane electric field and the incorporation of insulating substrates, enabling precise control of the valley degrees of freedom and associated topological phases. We identify a regime in which the valley degeneracy is lifted: one valley retains a gapless, linear Dirac-like dispersion, whereas the other develops a finite band gap and becomes electronically inactive. The interplay between Floquet driving and inversion-symmetry breaking induces topological phase transitions characterized by Chern numbers C = -2, C = -1, and C = 0, together with the emergence of perfectly valley-polarized domain-wall channels. Furthermore, magnetic asymmetry arising from proximity to adjacent two-dimensional ferromagnetic contacts enables spin-valley filtering. These findings establish the potential of graphene-based heterostructures as highly tunable systems for controlling spin and valley degrees of freedom.

papers.title: Topological phases protected by half-chiral symmetry
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26693v1

summary.background:
- Topological phase: a property of a material's electronic structure that stays the same under smooth changes, often producing protected edge or corner states.
- Sublattice (chiral) symmetry: in a lattice split into two interleaved sets of sites, hopping only between the sets; this makes zero-energy edge states robust.
- Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain: a simple one-dimensional model of such a chain, a standard example.
- Hamiltonian: the matrix describing a system's energies and how particles hop between sites.
- Projection P: a mathematical operator that selects the states on one sublattice; the constraint PHP=0 means no direct hopping within that sublattice.
- Higher-order topology: edge states that appear at corners or hinges rather than along full edges.
- Graphene and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN): atomically thin honeycomb-lattice materials; Kekulé distortion is a pattern that changes hopping strengths on the honeycomb.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes topological phases protected by "half-chiral" symmetry, where the sublattice (chiral) symmetry holds on only one sublattice, and builds a real-space invariant framework with a 2D Kekulé honeycomb model showing higher-order corner modes.
summary.plain: Some materials have atoms arranged on two interlocking sublattices, and a special symmetry normally pins down their edge behavior. This paper looks at the case where that symmetry holds on only one of the two sublattices, which can happen when the sublattices are unequal or when orbitals are localized. The authors describe a new way to classify such systems and show, in a two-dimensional model, that a single zero-energy state can be stuck to one corner.
summary.why: It extends the well-known idea of topology protected by sublattice symmetry to a weaker, algebraic constraint that group-theory methods do not cover, which may matter for materials like graphene on hexagonal boron nitride. The text does not report experiments or quantify practical impact, so its wider significance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Chiral (or sublattice) symmetry describes bipartite systems such as the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain where same-sublattice A-A and B-B hoppings are forbidden, enabling the protection of topological phases. Here we identify new topological phases protected by half-chiral symmetry wherein chiral symmetry is preserved on only one sublattice, as may occur with sublattice imbalance (e.g. graphene-hBN) or localized orbitals (e.g. zincblende). Unlike conventional symmetry operators described by group theory, half-chiral symmetry is an algebraic constraint on the sublattice-projected Hamiltonian such as $PHP=0$, requiring a new framework for topological protection. We develop such a framework, identifying real-space bulk topological invariants and corresponding topological boundary modes that stick to zero energy. In two dimensions we construct a half-chiral Kekule honeycomb model and show that its unusual higher-order topology protects a single zero-energy mode at a single corner.

papers.title: Comparing weakly interacting and free quantum dynamics locally
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27707v1

summary.background:
- Quantum many-body system: many interacting particles whose joint state is described by quantum mechanics.
- Lieb-Robinson bound: a mathematical limit showing that effects spread through a lattice system at a finite speed, roughly like a light cone.
- Non-interacting (one-body) dynamics: each particle evolves on its own, which is much easier to analyze.
- Quantum diffusion: spreading that grows with time in the way heat or ink spreads, here measured by an operator spreading diagnostic.
- Out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC): a correlation function used to measure how quickly quantum information scrambles.
- Fermi-Hubbard model: a standard lattice model of interacting electrons.
- Perturbative regime: results valid when interactions or disorder are weak and times are not too long.
summary.one_liner: Using Lieb-Robinson bounds to show that weakly interacting many-body quantum dynamics can be locally approximated by free (non-interacting) one-body dynamics on large perturbative time scales, yielding quantum diffusion results for weakly interacting Fermi systems and free-correlation approximations for Fermi-Hubbard models with low spin-down density.
summary.plain: This paper studies how quantum particles spread out and interact in a crowd. It shows that, for weak interactions and for a limited time, the complicated many-particle behavior can be locally replaced by a simpler version where the particles do not interact. Using this replacement, the authors prove that spreading behaves diffusively in certain systems and that some correlation patterns match their non-interacting counterparts.
summary.why: It gives a rigorous way to transfer known results for simple non-interacting systems to interacting ones over finite times, which matters for understanding how quantum information spreads. The text does not indicate direct experimental or applied consequences, and its link to the numerical work by Bippus et al. is described only as a counterpart, not as a confirmation.

papers.abstract: Lieb-Robinson bounds (LRBs) have become a standard tool for perturbative results in quantum many-body physics, including gap stability and many-body adiabatic theory. Here, we use LRBs to locally approximate weakly interacting many-body dynamics with one-body dynamics on large, perturbative time scales. This allows us to use one-body transport results to establish the expected many-body transport behavior on finite time scales in the following two illustrative settings: (i) We prove quantum diffusion, as quantified by a certain operator spreading diagnostic, in weakly interacting and weakly disordered Fermi systems in dimensions $D\geq2$ on large finite time scales based on the non-interacting diffusion result of Black, Drogin, and Hern\'andez [arXiv:2506.06468]. (ii) We show for Fermi-Hubbard models with initially low spin-down density, that all local multi-time spin-up correlation functions are approximated by their free counterparts. In particular, we obtain an OTOC (out-of-time-ordered correlator) counterpart to the patterns of short-time entanglement related to lattice path counts observed numerically by Bippus et al. [Phys. Rev. B 113, 035152 (2026)].

papers.title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26604v1

summary.background:
- Hubbard model: a simple lattice model of electrons that hop between sites and repel each other when two share a site; U is the repulsion and t the hopping strength.
- Strongly correlated electrons: electrons whose interactions are too strong for simple single-particle pictures to work.
- Hole doping: removing some electrons from a half-filled system, here 1/8 of the expected filling.
- Variational energy: an upper bound on the ground-state energy from a trial quantum state; lower is better.
- Tensor networks (PEPS): a way of compressing a many-particle quantum state into a grid of small linked arrays; contraction cost is the computing effort needed to evaluate it.
- Gaussian states: quantum states whose correlations follow simple pairing rules, easy to compute with but limited in expressiveness.
- Neural network quantum states: using a neural network as a trial wavefunction optimized numerically.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), a tensor-network ansatz with exact contraction cost O(N^{3/2}) on 2D lattices, and applies it to the Hubbard model at U/t=8 and 1/8 hole doping on lattices up to 1024 sites.
summary.plain: Physicists want to predict how many interacting electrons behave inside a material, but exact calculations blow up quickly as the system grows. This paper proposes a new mathematical form for describing the electrons' quantum state that mixes neural networks with a simpler "Gaussian" building block. The authors report that it gives low-energy estimates on grids of up to 1024 sites for a standard model of electrons (the Hubbard model).
summary.why: Strongly correlated electrons underlie phenomena such as high-temperature superconductivity, which is why accurate simulations matter, though the text itself does not make that link. The reported scaling and the large system sizes suggest the method may be practical where many existing approaches struggle, but the text does not compare costs or accuracy against specific alternatives in enough detail to judge its importance.

papers.abstract: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of $O(N^{3/2})$ on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at $U/t=8$ and $1/8$ hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.

papers.title: Topology-Enabled Self-Verification of Quantum Hall Resistance Standards
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26016v1

summary.background:
- Quantum Hall effect: in a two-dimensional electron system at low temperature and strong magnetic field, resistance takes exact, universally reproducible values set by fundamental constants.
- Resistance array standard: many quantum Hall elements wired together to reach resistance values useful for calibration.
- Quantization breakdown: a localized failure where the exact quantized value stops holding inside part of the device.
- Edge states: conducting channels along the device boundary that carry current without loss; verifying them directly is the conventional check the paper aims to avoid.
- Cn symmetry: a design with n-fold rotational symmetry, which the proposed criterion relies on.
- Outer terminal measurements: electrical readings taken only at the device's external contacts.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a statistical reliability criterion, the Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability (SPQR) criterion, that aims to verify quantum Hall array resistance standards using only outer-terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric device designs.
summary.plain: Quantum Hall devices are used as very precise electrical resistance references, and larger arrays of them are harder to check for hidden faults where the quantized behavior breaks down inside the device. This paper describes a mathematical framework that aims to give statistical assurance of such faults being unlikely by measuring only at the outer terminals, rather than relying on checking the edge-state currents directly.
summary.why: Precision resistance standards underpin electrical measurement, so a way to validate large arrays without invasive checks could matter for metrology. The text also suggests possible uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing, but it does not show results for those areas, so that connection remains unverified.

papers.abstract: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport. One proposed solution is to use a Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability criterion, a mathematical framework that statistically assures such validation strictly through outer terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric designs. This criterion essentially bounds the likelihood of hidden localized defects arising from quantum Hall breakdown and has potential uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing but is presented in the context of its application toward quantum electrical standards.

papers.title: Quantum many-body scars and zero modes in the spin-1 Kitaev chain
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25051v1

summary.background:
- Quantum spin: a tiny magnetic degree of freedom; spin-1 means three possible states per site.
- Kitaev chain: a one-dimensional model of interacting spins with direction-dependent couplings.
- Zero modes: states with exactly zero energy; chiral symmetry is a mathematical symmetry that protects them.
- Hilbert-space connectivity: which basis states can be reached from which others by the dynamics.
- Quantum many-body scars: special non-thermal states that show slow, repeating dynamics instead of scrambling.
- PXP model: a standard toy model in which scars were first studied; FSA is an approximation that maps the dynamics onto a simpler effective hopping problem.
- Tight-binding: a simple model of particles hopping between neighbouring sites.
- Jacobsthal number: an integer sequence; here it gives a lower bound on the zero-mode count.
summary.one_liner: The paper finds exponentially many exact zero-energy modes protected by chiral symmetry in the spin-1 Kitaev chain, and identifies an embedded tight-binding defect structure that gives PXP-like quantum many-body scars in several sectors, described by a universal forward-scattering approximation Hamiltonian.
summary.plain: This paper studies a chain of tiny quantum magnets (spin-1 particles) arranged in a line, with a specific pattern of interactions. The authors show the chain has a very large number of special states that do not change energy over time, and they find that some other special states keep returning to their starting pattern when the system is run forward. They explain much of this with a simple picture of defects moving between barriers.
summary.why: Quantum many-body scars are unusual states that resist the usual tendency of isolated quantum systems to scramble and heat up, which matters for quantum simulation and quantum computing. The text reports a counting result and an analytic construction, but its wider significance beyond this model is not established in the excerpt provided.

papers.abstract: We study the spin-1 Kitaev chain and, by analyzing its Hilbert-space connectivity in the Cartesian basis, show that it hosts an exponentially large number of exact zero-energy modes protected by chiral symmetry. For even-length periodic chains, their count is lower-bounded by the Jacobsthal number $(2^{L+1}+1)/3$, where $L$ is the chain length. We then construct an exponentially large number ($2^{L/2}$) of zero modes with an analytic expression that have a maximally mixed density matrix for a contiguous bipartition using the operator-state mapping. We further identify an embedded tight-binding structure governing defect dynamics that supports PXP-like quantum many-body scars (QMBS) in multiple sectors previously not reported. The associated forward-scattering approximation (FSA) Hamiltonian takes a universal form across the scarred sectors studied. A simple physical picture of defects propagating between walls provides an intuitive description of these dynamics and a structural guide to identifying sectors with fidelity revivals, while its limitations point to additional scarring mechanisms.

papers.title: Exact Parent Hamiltonians for Partially Magnetized Chiral Spin Liquids
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24935v1

summary.background:
- Spin liquid: a magnet whose spins stay disordered and entangled even at very low temperature.
- Chiral spin liquid: a spin liquid that breaks time-reversal symmetry, giving it a definite handedness.
- Topological order: a kind of order described by global patterns of entanglement, not by local symmetry breaking; it can carry fractional excitations.
- Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states: electron or boson states in strong magnetic fields with fractionally charged excitations; "Abelian" and "non-Abelian" refer to how those excitations exchange statistics.
- Parent Hamiltonian: an engineered local energy function whose exact ground state is a target wavefunction.
- Kalmeyer-Laughlin state: the original chiral spin liquid model, which this work generalizes.
- Hubbard model: a lattice model of particles hopping between sites with an on-site repulsion; the limit of infinite repulsion removes doubly occupied sites.
- Superexchange: an effective spin-spin interaction arising at second order from virtual electron hopping.
summary.one_liner: The paper constructs exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized chiral spin liquids realizing bosonic topological orders, via a Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall states taken to infinite on-site repulsion and mapped onto spins.
summary.plain: The paper concerns a exotic magnetic state of matter called a chiral spin liquid, in which spins are strongly entangled and do not order, yet carry a built-in handedness. The authors write down simple, exactly solvable model rules (Hamiltonians) that have these states as their ground states, by starting from a known exactly solvable model of bosons in a lattice version of the fractional quantum Hall effect and translating it into spin language. They also outline how such spin models might be realized in electron systems with tailored hoppings and interactions, though the text presents these as derivations rather than experiments.
summary.why: Exact, solvable models are valuable benchmarks because they let researchers study topological order without approximations, and this work extends the classic Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin model to a wider family of bosonic states, including non-Abelian ones. Its relevance to real materials or quantum devices is not established by the text alone, so that connection should be treated as speculative.

papers.abstract: Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are paradigmatic fractionalized phases, yet simple exact parent Hamiltonians for them remain scarce. In this work, we construct exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs realizing various bosonic topological orders. Our construction relies on an exact Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, valid at arbitrary repulsive interaction strengths. Taking the on-site repulsion to infinity and applying local boson-spin mappings yields exact parent Hamiltonians for the CSLs. Our two-spin construction generalizes the Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin Hamiltonian to a broader class of bosonic FQH model states, including Abelian states and non-Abelian parton states. We derive controlled microscopic realizations of these two-spin Hamiltonians via second-order superexchange in generalized spinful Hofstadter-Hubbard models with tailored hoppings and interactions. With more general local constraints and interactions, boson-spin mappings yield exact higher-spin and multispin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs.

papers.title: Intrinsic second-order nonlinear Hall effect from perturbation theory
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22229v1

summary.background:
- Hall effect: a sideways current or voltage produced by a field, classically from a magnetic field; the "nonlinear" version here arises without one, from the crystal's electronic structure.
- Nonlinear response: the output is not proportional to the input; a second-order term scales with the field squared.
- Bloch electrons: electrons in a periodic crystal, described by states labeled by momentum.
- Quantum geometry: properties of electron states, such as Berry curvature, that depend on how states change with momentum.
- Perturbation theory: solving a problem by expanding in powers of a small quantity (here the applied field) and solving order by order.
- Distribution function: the statistical occupancy of electron states in momentum space.
- Wavepacket theory: an alternative approach that treats electrons as localized packets of states.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives the intrinsic second-order nonlinear Hall conductivity from a textbook-style perturbation expansion of the Bloch-state velocity and distribution function, and checks it against wavepacket-based theories.
summary.plain: The paper is about how electrons in a crystal carry current in a sideways (Hall) direction when the applied electric field is strong enough that the response is no longer simply proportional to the field. Instead of relying on more specialized wavepacket methods, the authors use a standard step-by-step (perturbation) calculation to work out this response. They report that the approach gives a well-defined result and that it is consistent with the existing wavepacket-based theories.
summary.why: The effect is described as independent of impurity scattering and tied to the quantum geometry of electron states, so it may serve as a probe of crystal symmetry and electronic structure. The text does not report new measured values, so its practical reach beyond clarifying the theory is unclear.

papers.abstract: Nonlinear transport provides an efficient probe of the electronic structure and symmetry of quantum materials. As a prominent example, the intrinsic nonlinear Hall effect has attracted considerable attention in recent years because it is independent of impurity scattering and directly reflects the quantum geometry of Bloch electrons. Here we establish a simple textbook-style perturbation theory for the intrinsic nonlinear conductivity. Based on the well-defined Bloch-state velocity, our formulation perturbatively determines the field-corrected velocity and distribution function, from which the conductivity follows directly. We further compare our approach with wavepacket-based theories and discuss their consistency.

papers.title: Hidden topological signatures in a van der Waals ferromagnet revealed by spin-resolved circular-dichroic photoemission
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24468v1

summary.background:
- Van der Waals material: a crystal built from layers that are weakly bonded to each other, so thin flakes can be peeled off.
- Ferromagnet: a material whose atomic magnetic moments align in one direction, below a transition temperature (here 58 K).
- Photoemission: shining light on a surface to eject electrons; measuring their energy and direction reveals the electronic band structure.
- Spin-resolved: also recording which way each ejected electron's spin points.
- Circular dichroism: a difference in response to left- versus right-handed (circularly polarized) light.
- Berry curvature and topology: mathematical properties of how electron states twist through momentum space; nonzero values are linked to topological effects.
- Time-reversal symmetry: the symmetry broken when a material becomes magnetic; its breaking is one signature the paper looks for.
- Density functional theory: a standard computer method for estimating electronic structure from first principles.
summary.one_liner: Spin- and angle-resolved photoemission, circular-dichroism measurements and density functional theory are used to map the spin-polarized electronic structure of the van der Waals ferromagnet Ni1/4TaSe2, reporting signs of broken time-reversal symmetry and a helicity-dependent spin response suggestive of local topological character.
summary.plain: This paper studies a layered magnetic material, Ni1/4TaSe2, which becomes ferromagnetic below about 58 K and sits close in composition to a superconducting version of the material. The authors used light shining on the surface to knock electrons out and measured their spin and momentum, and they compared the results with computer calculations. They report spin-polarized electrons near the energy level that controls electrical behavior, plus a response to light polarization that they interpret as a sign of topological character.
summary.why: The work links magnetism, electron spin and possible topology in one material, which the text suggests may bear on why superconductivity appears when nickel is depleted. That connection is stated as a motivation for future work; the text does not show it, so its relevance to superconductivity remains unconfirmed.

papers.abstract: Layered ferromagnets with strongly correlated electrons provide a platform for exploring the interplay among magnetism, spin-orbit coupling, and nontrivial band topology. $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$ is a correlated van der Waals ferromagnet with a transition temperature of 58 K that lies close in composition to a superconducting phase that emerges upon Ni depletion. Here, we combine spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, circular-dichroism measurements, and density functional theory calculations to investigate its spin-resolved electronic structure. We observe spin-polarized states crossing the Fermi level and signatures of broken time-reversal symmetry in the ferromagnetic state. Spin-resolved circular-dichroism measurements further reveal a helicity-dependent spin response consistent with a finite spin Berry curvature and suggestive of local topological character. Together, these results establish an experimental connection between ferromagnetism, spin-polarized electronic states, and topological signatures in $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$, providing a foundation for investigating how these properties may relate to the emergence of superconductivity upon Ni depletion.

papers.title: Constraints on the volume enclosed by Fermi surfaces
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21720v1

summary.background:
- Fermi surface: the boundary in momentum space separating occupied from empty electron states; its enclosed volume can be measured in some experiments.
- Fermi liquid: the standard model of metals, where electrons behave like weakly interacting particles.
- Luttinger's theorem: the classic result that the Fermi-surface volume equals the electron density in a Fermi liquid.
- Quantum spin liquid: a magnetic material whose spins do not freeze into order even at very low temperature, with fractional excitations called spinons.
- Parton gauge theory: a method of writing electrons or spins as combinations of simpler particles tied together by an emergent gauge field.
- Flux insertion (Oshikawa's argument): a thought experiment threading magnetic flux through a ring of material to constrain allowed states.
summary.one_liner: A review that extends Luttinger's proof of the Fermi-surface volume in ordinary Fermi liquids to fractionalized Fermi liquids (FL*) described by parton gauge theories, and discusses Oshikawa's flux-insertion arguments including gapless spin liquids.
summary.plain: The paper is about how many electrons' worth of states are enclosed by the boundary (Fermi surface) between filled and empty electron energies in a metal-like quantum material. In an ordinary metal the enclosed volume is fixed by the electron density alone. In a more exotic state, where electrons split into pieces called spinons, the same rule holds but with the density shifted by a fixed whole number, and the review works out why using a generalized version of an old proof.
summary.why: This sets out a precise counting rule that tells experimentalists and theorists what Fermi-surface size to expect in exotic quantum spin liquids, which can help test whether such a state is present. The text does not indicate specific experimental results or claims beyond the theory itself.

papers.abstract: A fundamental property of a Fermi liquid (FL) is that the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by $ρ$, the total density of electrons. In a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*), the volume enclosed by the Fermi surface is determined by the same expression after $ρ$ has been shifted by a quantized amount, most commonly to $ρ-1$ (we assume spin rotation invariance, for simplicity). The FL* shift is related to the quantized symmetry fractionalization data of a quantum spin liquid, whose fractionalized spinon excitations are present alongside the Fermi surface quasiparticles. In this review article, we establish the FL* Fermi volume by generalizing the original Luttinger proof for FL to parton gauge theories of the quantum spin liquid and FL*. We also discuss Oshikawa's flux insertion arguments for FL, and their extension to FL*, including a discussion of gapless spin liquids.

papers.title: Topological phase diagram of an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with negative coupling
papers.label: arXiv:2611.18456v1

summary.background:
- Topological phase: a property of a system's band structure that stays the same under smooth changes, often linked to edge states at boundaries.
- Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model: a simple one-dimensional chain of sites with alternating hopping strengths, a standard textbook example of topology.
- Unit cell: the repeating group of sites; here each contains three atoms (sites).
- Bands and wave vector k: energy levels of waves in a periodic lattice, labeled by momentum k; the k=0 point is the centre of the Brillouin zone.
- Zak phase: a number computed from a band's wavefunctions over the Brillouin zone that signals its topology in one dimension.
- Exciton-polariton: a hybrid of light and matter excitations in a semiconductor microcavity.
- Phase diagram: a map showing which topological phase occurs for each combination of parameters.
summary.one_liner: An analytic phase diagram for an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with three atoms per unit cell and negative coupling, mapping seven regions with four topological phases via Zak phases of the three bands.
summary.plain: The paper studies a model of waves hopping along a chain of repeating units, a simplified description of a structure recently built from light-matter particles (exciton-polaritons) in perovskite micropillars. The authors work out, by calculation, how the system's topological character changes as two parameters are varied: the energy offset between sites and the ratio of hopping strengths between and within units. They report seven regions in this parameter plane, falling into four distinct topological phases.
summary.why: The text notes that the second and third bands swap topological character through a band crossing tied to a negative coupling, a feature specific to this experimental system. The phase diagram is meant to help interpret existing experiments and guide future ones, though the text does not report experimental comparisons itself.

papers.abstract: Recently, an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with three atoms per unit cell has been experimentally realized in perovskite exciton-polariton micropillars. A distinctive feature of this system is that the second and third bands undergo a topological transition through a band crossing at the wave vector $k=0$, associated with a negative coupling. In this work, we analytically determine the phase diagram of the model as a function of the on-site energy splitting and the ratio of intercell to intracell hopping amplitudes. We identify seven regions in this lane, with four distinct topological phases, characterized by different Zak phases of the three bands. Our results provide a useful theoretical framework for interpreting existing experiments and serve as a guide for future experimental investigations of this system.
